newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Medicaid asset transfer needs repeal - Vladeck.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Medicaid asset transfer needs repeal - Vladeck.

text.p: A Clinton administration official said Tuesday that Congress should roll back a provision of a new insurance law setting criminal penalties for people who transfer assets expressly to qualify for Medicaid nursing home care.
The provision is part of a popular law, signed by President Clinton last August, helping individuals keep health insurance if they change jobs or have a pre-existing illness.
Medicaid is a state-federal health program that serves 37 million poor, elderly and disabled individuals.
To qualify for nursing home care, individuals must meet income and assets tests. Medicaid pays half the nation's nursing home bills.
Congress has tried in the past to crack down on people who transfer or "spend down" assets to qualify for Medicaid and thus avoid paying higher private rates for nursing home care.
The new law set out criminal penalties, including jail, for people who "knowingly and willfully" dispose of assets in order to receive Medicaid.

"There needs to be a provision to repal the criminalization of asset transfers," said Bruce Vladeck, administrator of the federal Health Care Financing Administration, told the Senate Labor Committee. He also said the administration would not press states to enforce the provision.

A consumer advocate said the new law has stirred fears among senior citizens who worry that giving financial gifts to adult children or grandchildren, or adding an adult child's name to a checking account could now be a felony.

"While we share the objective of Congress to preserve Medicaid funds for the truly needy, we are deeply troubled by the propsect of...the transfer of elderly nursing home rsidents from their nursing home to prison," Gail Shearer of the Consumers Union said in a statement.
She said lawyers had run advertisements in an Arizona newspaper warning individuals that without proper advice, they could make a mistake that could get them tossed into jail.

Shearer said Congress should clarify the law to ensure that felony charges, steep fines and imprisonment would not apply to individuals who were merely trying to assure their bills will be paid if they become incapacitated.
